definition: The Massachusetts regulation prohibiting unnecessary or excessive noise from man-made sources, treating noise as air pollution.
The FAA's long-standing threshold: homes, schools, hospitals and similar uses are considered incompatible with airport noise at or above it.
A filter that turns down bass and extreme treble to mimic human hearing; the default for nearly all environmental and workplace noise rules.
A 2021 California law halting the sale of most new gas leaf blowers, mowers and other small off-road engines by 2024.
A UK council order requiring a statutory nuisance to stop or be limited; ignoring one is an offence.
A crosswalk signal that gives walk information by sound and vibration as well as sight, for blind and low-vision pedestrians.
Under OSHA, an 85 dBA 8-hour TWA (a 50% dose) at which employers must run a hearing conservation program.
The FAA model airports must use to produce noise contours for Part 150 studies.
Planning principle that makes whoever arrives second - new homes beside a venue, or a new venue beside homes - pay to manage the noise between them.
The sound level present without the noise being complained about; some codes limit how far a source may rise above it.
A reversing alarm that adjusts its loudness to stay just above background; the Big Dig capped it at 5 dBA over background.
A health outcome in noise research measured with standardized surveys; the EEA estimates almost 16.9 million Europeans are long-term annoyed by transport noise.
The 2020 global slowdown in human activity during COVID-19 lockdowns, when human-made noise dropped sharply.
Boston's Air Pollution Control Commission, which writes the city's technical noise regulations, including zoning-district, octave-band and construction limits.
Hawaii's one-minute steady outdoor siren tone, used in statewide siren tests.
A dip in a hearing test pattern that suggests noise damage; CDC found one in 24.4% of US adults aged 20 to 69.
The artificial warning sound EU rules require on electric and hybrid vehicles up to about 20 km/h and in reverse.
Japan's municipal disaster-radio loudspeaker network, tested daily with an evening tune such as "Yuyake Koyake."
A reverse alarm that hisses across many frequencies instead of beeping; OSHA said in 2004 it can comply with federal rules.
How much air a turbofan's fan pushes around the engine core compared with through it; higher ratios mean slower, cooler, quieter exhaust.
A much flatter filter that keeps the bass; commonly used for peak measurements and bass-heavy sources.
The Central Artery/Tunnel project's construction noise specification, the source of the FHWA's equipment spec limits.
Ringing a set of tuned bells in mathematical sequences rather than melodies, as at Old North Church.
The Boston ordinance setting 50 dBA from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. and 70 dBA at other times; nuisance citations do not require scientific measurement.
IEC 61672 grades for precision and general-purpose sound level meters; the older US terms are Type 1 and Type 2.
A body created by the state legislature to advise Massport, representing 35 communities.
Lower-level area at an event where audiences can rest their ears; Switzerland requires 85 dB(A) or less for long loud events, and AAO-HNS recommends 70 dB LAeq,15min or less.
Equipment that sheds heat by evaporating water; at data centers, up to 70 dBA within 400 feet according to EESI.
Electrical discharge into the air around high-voltage conductors, which can make power lines hum.
The speed above which tire-on-pavement noise becomes louder than engine noise; about 20 mph (32 km/h) for cars, higher for trucks.
Hours when an airport is closed to most flights, such as Sydney's 11 pm-6 am curfew.
Burst of birdsong around first light; a Leiden study found urban birds start it 22 minutes earlier on average than rural birds.
The EU 24-hour average with +5 dB added in the evening (19:00-23:00) and +10 dB at night (23:00-07:00) by default.
A US 24-hour, A-weighted average that counts sound from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. as 10 dB louder; the FAA's standard aviation metric.
Sound level with C-weighting, which counts bass more fully than A-weighting; used to cap low-frequency sound at shows, such as France's 118 dB(C) limit.
Decibels adjusted to roughly match human hearing, de-emphasizing low bass; the unit used in US workplace noise limits.
Decibels measured with a flatter filter that keeps bass; some codes use it to limit thumping music.
A logarithmic unit comparing a sound's pressure with a reference of 20 micropascals; +3 dB doubles the energy and about +10 dB sounds twice as loud.
Reducing a protector's labeled NRR to estimate real protection, such as OSHA's subtract-7 method or NIOSH's 50% for foam plugs.
German standard for sound warning devices on authorized emergency vehicles; current edition March 2022.
The FAA's annual airport noise metric, with a 65 dB significance threshold that the FAA's Noise Policy Review examined.
Two periodical cicada broods emerging in the same year, as Broods XIII and XIX did in 2024 for the first time in 221 years.
A truck engine mode that changes exhaust valve timing so the engine absorbs power to slow the truck; loud with poor or straight-pipe mufflers.
The 2002 EU law requiring strategic noise maps and action plans on a five-year cycle, without EU-wide limits.
How many decibels of increase halves the allowed exposure time: 3 dB for NIOSH, 5 dB for OSHA.
US rule that motorcycles built after 1982 carry chassis and muffler labels with matching codes; a mismatch on a regulated bike violates the Noise Control Act.
Greasing the wheel flange or rail to reduce squeal; cut levels by 8 to 11 dB in a French trial.
Sound traveling around a wall through floors, slabs or stud cavities instead of through it.
US federal safety standard requiring hybrid and electric vehicles to make sound when stopped in gear, in reverse and up to 30 km/h.
How many pressure cycles pass per second, heard as pitch; human hearing runs from about 20 Hz to 10,000-20,000 Hz.
A product applied to the top of the rail to control wheel-rail friction and reduce squeal; results vary by site.

term: Global standard for safe listening venues and events
definition: Voluntary 2022 WHO standard with six features, led by a 100 dB LAeq,15min audience limit, plus monitoring, better acoustics, hearing protection, quiet zones and staff training.
How many times per second alternating current reverses: 60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in much of the world.
Hum in audio equipment at the line frequency itself (50 or 60 Hz), rather than at double it.
Tones at multiples of a fundamental frequency; mains hum has strong harmonics that make it sound buzzy.
A short tune, about seven seconds, played at Japanese stations before a train departs.
The direction-dependent filtering of sound by the outer ear and head, one of the cues the brain uses to locate a sound.
Years of healthy life lost to illness, disability or early death; the EEA estimates 1.5 million a year from transport noise in Europe.
Siren tone that alternates between two fixed pitches.
Survey category for people choosing the top of an annoyance scale; used to link noise levels to community reaction.
A hydraulic breaking hammer mounted on an excavator arm; measured at 90 dBA Lmax at 50 feet in the FHWA table.
Citizen-science app developed by Antonella Radicchi at TU Berlin for mapping peaceful places; used in Berlin and Limerick quiet-area planning.
Per ICD-10 H93.23, an abnormally disproportionate increase in the sensation of loudness in response to sounds of normal volume.
How many decibels a noise wall removes compared with no wall; about 5 to 10 dBA for homes directly behind one.
A 2019 voluntary standard for phones and headphones that tracks a weekly sound allowance (80 dB for 40 hours a week for adults).
The sound level exceeded 10 percent of the time during a measurement - a measure of the louder moments. Boston's construction limits use it.
The levels exceeded 10% and 90% of the time; L10 is used for traffic, L90 for background sound.
The level exceeded 90% of the time during a measurement; a common measure of background noise.
The steady A-weighted level with the same sound energy as a fluctuating sound over a set time, such as 15 minutes or 24 hours.
A-weighted equivalent (average) sound level over 15 minutes; the measure used by the WHO venue standard and France's legal cap.
The maximum A-weighted sound level, with fast time weighting, during a single event such as a drone pass.
The highest A-weighted sound level during an event; the UK proposed 95 dB LAmax at 7.5 m for noise cameras.
The highest A-weighted level measured with the meter's fast time response; AAO-HNS uses it for peak caps of 140 dB (adults) and 120 dB (children).
Sideways slip of a wheel across the railhead on a curve; the most important cause of curve squeal.
A 24-hour average sound level with penalties for evening and night noise; the EU uses it to map road, rail and aircraft noise.
The steady level that would carry the same total sound energy as a fluctuating sound over the same period.
The steady sound level carrying the same energy as the actual fluctuating sound over one hour; used in US federal highway noise rules.
The highest sound level reached during a measurement - the peak moment, not an average.
The average sound level over the night period, used in EU noise maps to estimate sleep disturbance.
A quiet tone repeating once per second during "don't walk" that helps pedestrians find the APS push button.
The automatic tendency to speak louder, and change pitch and pace, in noise.
The low-pitched part of a sound; a 2018 Arup study found gas blowers have much more of it than electric ones, which helps them carry.
The highest instantaneous sound pressure, measured with no time averaging.
Flying supersonic at a speed and altitude where the boom bends upward before reaching the ground.
The slight change in shape of iron or steel in a magnetic field; it makes transformer cores vibrate and hum.
The drone from electrical equipment tied to grid frequency, centered on 120 Hz on 60 Hz grids and 100 Hz on 50 Hz grids.
The German two-tone emergency horn, defined by DIN 14610 and the only warning tone German priority vehicles may use.
The rule that a wall blocks about 6 dB more for each doubling of its mass or of the sound's frequency, so bass gets through more easily.
MassDEP's 1990 guidance: a source violates 310 CMR 7.10 if it raises sound 10 dBA above ambient L90, or creates a pure tone, at the property line and nearest receptor.
New York City Office of Nightlife program that uses mediation instead of enforcement for venue-neighbor disputes; reports an 80% resolution rate.
Per a 2022 consensus definition, a disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds or their associated stimuli.
UK Pop Code measure of concert noise at neighbors: a 15-minute LAeq taken 1 m from the facade of noise-sensitive homes.
FAA national survey (mailed from October 2015 around 20 airports) whose 2021 results showed far more annoyance than the Schultz Curve.
City official or appointee who works between nightlife businesses, residents and city government.
A free iOS app from the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, accurate to about 2 dBA with the built-in mic in lab tests.
US federal highway noise levels in 23 CFR 772 (67 dBA Leq(h) outside homes) that trigger consideration of noise walls.
A roadside sound meter linked to a license plate camera that records vehicles above a set level.
US class of the maximum noise a new aircraft type may make, set in 14 CFR Part 36; ICAO groups equivalent limits into Chapters.
A line on an airport noise map joining points of equal sound level, like a topographic line.
A computer model of long-term average sound levels from roads, rail and aircraft, not a direct measurement.
A New York City-required plan for how a construction site will reduce noise, needed for every after-hours authorization.
A local law setting when and how loud sounds may be; in Canada usually called a bylaw.
FAA review opened May 2023 of whether to keep DNL and the 65 DNL threshold; awaiting an advisory committee report as of October 2026.
The EPA-required lab rating on US hearing protectors, on labels since 1979; real-world protection is usually lower.
Hearing loss caused by loud sound; NIDCD calls it the only completely preventable type of hearing loss.
An app from BU's Community Noise Lab that pairs sound readings with how a sound makes people feel on a live map.
The usual US method for measuring tire noise, using microphones mounted a few inches from a rolling test tire.
A slice of the frequency spectrum, such as 63 Hz or 1,000 Hz; Boston's APCC rules set a separate limit for each band from 31.5 Hz to 8,000 Hz.

term: Office of Noise Abatement and Control
definition: The EPA office created to carry out the Noise Control Act of 1972; Congress stopped funding it in 1981.
An asphalt with connected air voids that absorb some tire noise; benefits vary widely and can fade within a few years.
Voluntary FAA program in which an airport maps its 65 DNL contour and proposes noise fixes that can qualify for federal grants.
Australian pedestrian push button designed in 1984 with a slow locator chirp, a rapid tick-tock to cross and a "kapow" on change.
Cicadas that emerge in huge numbers on 13- or 17-year cycles; choruses have been reported at 90-100 dB.
OSHA's enforceable US workplace noise limit, 90 dBA over 8 hours with a 5 dB exchange rate.
A very rapid electronic siren sweep, one of the standard tones on electronic sirens.
A rule broken if a sound can be clearly heard at a set distance or place, with no meter needed.
A loudness measure for booms based on human hearing; NASA's X-59 targets under 75 PLdB on the ground.
Where a noise is measured for enforcement, usually the complainant's property line or inside their home.
A single spot that loses about 6 dB per doubling of distance, versus a long stream like a highway that loses about 3 dB.

aka: Code of Practice on Environmental Noise Control at Concerts
definition: The UK Noise Council's 1995 code for outdoor concert noise at nearby homes, with limits from 09:00 to 23:00 and inaudibility indoors after 23:00.
A measurement of neighborhood sound before a facility is built; Chandler, Arizona requires one for data centers.
When a higher level of government's rule blocks a lower one from setting a different rule; federal EPA product noise standards preempt different local product standards.
Unit of sonic boom overpressure; the FAA's 2026 proposal would cap booms at the surface at 0.11 psf.
A noise dominated by one pitch, such as a whine or hum, which the MassDEP Noise Policy treats as a violation condition in itself.
Area a city can designate and protect from noise under the EU Environmental Noise Directive.
Times, usually overnight, when stricter noise limits apply, such as 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. in Boston.
A stretch of rail line, generally at least half a mile long, where trains do not routinely sound horns at crossings after added safety measures.
A points budget for night flights in which noisier aircraft cost more points; used at Heathrow since 1993.
The fast percussive walk indication on US accessible pedestrian signals, 10 repetitions per second.
The Federal Highway Administration's model for predicting construction noise, built on a table of equipment noise levels at 50 feet.
NIOSH's health-based workplace noise limit, 85 dBA over 8 hours with a 3 dB exchange rate; advice, not law.
A train wheel with rubber layers between hub and rim to damp vibration; does not guarantee an end to squeal.
The alarm OSHA requires on construction vehicles with an obstructed rear view unless a spotter signals the vehicle back.
Satellite-based navigation that lets aircraft fly precise paths; at Logan since 2014 it concentrated Runway 33L departures over the same neighborhoods.
A precision navigation procedure that allows curved approaches; Logan's curved Runway 33L RNP approach was implemented in 2021.
Federal Signal add-on that plays a low-frequency (182-400 Hz) copy of the siren through extra speakers so it can be felt inside cars; runs in eight-second bursts.
SAE recommended practice for laboratory testing of single-speaker electronic and electromechanical emergency vehicle sirens.
Older dose-response curve linking noise level to percent highly annoyed, based on data behind the 65 DNL policy; showed 12.3% highly annoyed at DNL 65.
A UK council notice setting hours and conditions on a construction site after a substantiated complaint.
A UK agreement on construction noise methods and hours made with the council before work starts, applied for at least 28 days ahead.
The Central Artery/Tunnel Project's construction noise specification, with background-based lot-line limits and per-machine emission limits at 50 ft.
Ground vibration picked up by seismometers, much of it from traffic, industry and people moving around; fell up to 50% at high frequencies during 2020 lockdowns.

term: Society for the Suppression of Unnecessary Noise
definition: The New York group founded by Julia Barnett Rice in 1906, which began with tugboat whistles near hospitals.
Shock wave from flying faster than sound, heard on the ground as a bang or thump.
One event's total sound energy expressed as if it had happened within one second.
A single-number wall rating averaged over 125-4,000 Hz, which can miss weak spots at lower bass frequencies.
The acoustic environment as people perceive or experience it, in context, as defined in ISO 12913-1 (2014).
A worker who signals that it is safe for a vehicle to reverse; OSHA's alternative to a reverse alarm.
In England and Wales, noise that unreasonably and substantially interferes with the use or enjoyment of a home or injures health; councils must act on it.
An EU-required, modeled map of long-term noise exposure from major roads, railways, airports and large cities, redone every five years.
A persistent low-frequency sound reported by some people in a place that others there cannot hear; most cases are unexplained.
Noise exposure averaged over a work shift, usually 8 hours.
Hearing ringing, buzzing or roaring with no outside source; a 2022 meta-analysis put adult prevalence at 14.4%.
Sound made where the tire tread meets the road surface; the main source of car noise at highway speeds.
FRA rule requiring locomotive horns 15-20 seconds before public grade crossings, at 96 to 110 dB(A), in a long-long-short-long pattern.
Jet engine with a large front fan that moves extra air around the core, reducing exhaust speed and jet noise.
UN test rule for quiet road transport vehicles: maximum 75 dBA at 10 and 20 km/h measured 2 m from center line, with pitch rising over 0.8% per km/h.
Quiet Parks International certification; the first went to Yangmingshan National Park, Taipei, in June 2020.
Swiss ordinance in force since June 2019 that regulates sound and laser exposure at events in tiers up to 100 dB(A) LAeq1h; replaced the 1996 Sound and Laser Ordinance.
A machine that drives piles by shaking them into the ground rather than hammering; measured at 101 dBA Lmax at 50 feet in the FHWA table.
Siren tone that rises and falls slowly in pitch; on a mechanical siren it comes from the rotor speeding up and slowing down.
The physical length of one sound cycle: the speed of sound divided by frequency, about 17 m at 20 Hz and 34 cm at 1 kHz.
A horn mounted at a gated crossing and aimed down the road, which may substitute for the train horn.
Public airport flight-tracking tool showing tracks, altitude, aircraft type and noise monitor readings, with a complaint button.
High-pitched noise from steel wheels slipping sideways on the rail in tight curves; up to about 100 dB(A) at 10 m.
A low rumble reported in Windsor, Ontario from about 2011, which a Canadian-funded study linked to blast furnaces on Zug Island, Michigan.
Siren tone that sweeps up and down much faster than the wail.
No weighting: a flat, unadjusted response between 10 Hz and 20 kHz.
An industrial island in River Rouge, Michigan, home to U.S. Steel blast furnaces identified as the likely source of the Windsor Hum.
